utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Mladic takes out his earphone, then there is no need to talk at the volume he is doing at this moment. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wanted to raise a matter. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours everyone in and around the courtroom. Yes, there is one preliminary matter. It relates to a revised translation for P00764, MFI. And that's 65 ter 08149. It has been uploaded into e-court under doc ID ZA01-9702-BCST and this is in relation to transcript pages 8272 to 8273 and transcript page 8278 on 2nd of February, 2013, as well as transcript page 9411 for the 28th of February, 2013. The Prosecution requests that the revised translation replace the existing translation in e-court and that the exhibit be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any comments, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm lost, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not, as a matter of fact, because I was prepared for this. It's just a matter of a better -- better translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Should we check it or?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we could do is to admit it and if you want to revisit the matter within the next 48 hours, you have an opportunity to do so. That seems to be the most efficient way of dealing with the matter. Then the Chamber hereby admits Exhibit P764 into evidence and instructs the Registrar to replace the current translation in e-court with the newly uploaded one. And the Defence has an opportunity if there are any problems to revisit the matter within 48 hours. Any other matter, Ms. Hasan?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We are ready to proceed with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the next witness will be Mr. Haglund, if I am well informed?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, a matter similar to the previous one. The Chamber notes that it was informed on the 11th of July through an informal communication that the Defence, following the Chamber's instructions of the 14th of December, 2012, has uploaded a more legible version of the English translation of Exhibit D123 into e-court. The Chamber hereby admits Exhibit D123 into evidence, under seal, and instructs the Registry to replace the current English translation in e-court with the newly uploaded one. If there would be any problem also for the Prosecution, there is an opportunity within the next 48 hours to revisit this matter if it has any concerns about the newly uploaded document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least I presume you are Mr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text of which is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Haglund, I have the habit of not addressing persons by title or rank but just by "mister" so it's not in any way in depreciation of the importance and relevance of titles and ranks. Mr. Haglund, you'll first be examined by Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan is counsel for the Prosecution and you find her to your right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Will you please state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: William Dale Haglund.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I see here that you have some documents, you have brought some documents with you. Can you please tell us what those are?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. They are the -- the three of them are the introductions to the reports, and then the third one was the Novo Kasaba and also that that includes the -- the pathology stuff, but I don't deal with that. I am not a pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. So we are clear, you have volume ones of all the sites that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes, I believe I have. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And now you have testified in this Tribunal in the Krstic case as well as in Popovic and in the Tolimir trial and recently on the 30th of January, 2012, in the Karadzic proceedings.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Have you recently had the opportunity to review your testimony that you gave in the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I read it last night, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly pause before answering the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund, you are invited to pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Ms. Hasan will do the same between answer and question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: On transcript page 3729 at lines 2 to 4 of your Krstic testimony, you were asked the following question, and I quote: "Q. Then in the summer of 1995, did you come over to be in charge of the exhumations for Bosnia? "A. That's correct." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, it's really 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now subject to that correction, if you were asked the same questions you were asked in the Krstic trial, would you provide this Chamber with the same information in substance?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, 1996 are when the exhumations were done.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And - sorry - in relation to the entirety of your Krstic testimony, if you were asked those questions that you -- that were put to you, would you provide the same information to this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And taking into account the correction as well, can you confirm that the evidence you gave was true and accurate to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd offer 65 ter 29115, which is -- which are excerpts of the transcript of testimony of Dr. Haglund from the Krstic trial into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have no objection, only to inform Your Honours that we received it late. We didn't know where to find it. I don't know. Maybe it can be checked. So I will in my cross address the original Krstic transcript. I didn't have time to switch to this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, any comments on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yeah. In fact, I'm a little bit confused. The Krstic testimony I'm referring to is what was attached to the 92 ter motion, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That dates of 24th of June?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I -- we received -- actually, in our list you can see it's -- it says the excerpts, but we really couldn't find one. But probably the pages are in order as it's in -- in the transcript, so I think everybody -- only we will use our 1D number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll try to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- because I don't know which is the statement which is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will try to find a co-ordinated approach. We will work with it but, of course, we also have to think about those who at a later stage will want to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The excerpts, apparently, are the excerpts as attachment to the 92 ter motion. We can proceed. And -- but first, Madam Registrar, the number of the excerpts from the transcript --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29115 receives number P1828, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, because there are quite a number of associated exhibits and other exhibits to be tendered, I propose to leave those until the end of the direct examination and proceed with the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Hasan. The Chamber is a bit concerned about the number of the pages in the associated exhibits, but let's see. And at this moment, certainly there is no opposition against waiting. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to call up 65 ter 29105. And, Your Honours, I will have to seek leave to add that to the Prosecution's 65 ter list. This is an updated CV from Dr. Haglund that was recently received.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Leave is granted. May I take it that you want to tender it?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, I -- yes, I will. I have just a few questions in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Doctor, is this a copy of your most recently CV that's up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 2 of the CV and page 4 of the B/C/S version, under "Field Experience," --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- we see that you've recently worked on exhumation projects in Granada, Cyprus, and Libya?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Libya was not a grave. I went there with Stefan Schmidt [phoen] to -- he was looking into how they could set up something for recovering remains, identifying remains, dealings with families, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now if we turn to page 4 in the English and 9 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: We see at the bottom of the page that you were the senior forensic advisor to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1996 in relation to Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage I'd offer 65 ter 29105 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29105 receives number P1829, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1829 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, in addition to testifying at this Tribunal you've also testified before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda as an expert witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And that was in the Kayishema and Rutaganda trials in 1997 and 1998 respectively?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now your evidence was relied on by the Trial Chamber in Kayishema but not in the case against Rutaganda due to some criticisms of your scientific method. Can you briefly explain to the Chamber what you know about those criticisms?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They were criticisms from a -- an American anthropologist. And in the United States we do things certain ways because we're very developed and have very good laboratories, et cetera, and some of the things that we wouldn't be able to do in Rwanda we couldn't do like we would in the United States. That was very much part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I can direct you to paragraphs 256 and 257 of the Rutaganda trial judgement, that's ICTR case 96-3-T, and it's dated 6 December 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now moving onto Bosnia, Dr. Haglund, you're probably one of the first persons who can tell us what it was really like working there in 1996. And specifically, if you could describe for us the security situation on the ground and what it is that you had to face?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The -- well, it wasn't -- our -- our laboratory where the autopsies were done and where the other anthropologists and other persons were working on the -- looking at the skeletal material and doing what they needed to do, that was held in Bosnia where people could walk around and -- and go out to the -- a restaurant or whatever. We were in the Serb side, basically, of Bosnia, and we stayed at a UN military base. When we needed -- when we went to work in the morning, we had jeeps with machine-guns and they had sent out small tanks early in the morning, and basically all the people that worked for me, they had to be in those convoys and I would -- was there most of the time with them, but -- so that was really tight for people. Is that the kind of answer that you needed with the -- okay, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So were you able to move around freely?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I did because I had to go back and forth to -- to the -- the other country up north, and -- but mostly I was with either the people in the laboratory but not as much, but most of the time I was with the graves.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And on a day-to-day basis, did you have any assurance from one day to the next whether you could go back to the sites and continue your work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think it was pretty well set up that we had the -- the people that were guarding us that -- it worked pretty well. It worked well.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I am going to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: But I note, Your Honours, that I went a little bit ahead of myself and I didn't read the summary for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You still have an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1996, Dr. Haglund oversaw the exhumation and examination of human remains from Srebrenica related mass graves at Cerska, Lazete 2, Pilica, also known as Branjevo military farm, and Nova Kasaba, graves 1 to 4. One hundred and fifty males were exhumed from the Cerska grave, of whom 149 died of gun-shot wounds. Forty-eight ligatures were recovered from that grave with about 24 of them still in place. The second site, Lazete 2, was located in a field behind a raised railway track underpass. Dr. Haglund located two deposits of bodies at the site which were designated Lazete 2A and 2B. Due to heavy rain, Dr. Haglund was unable to determine whether these two deposits were located in separate pits or formed one large trench. Lazete 2 was an undisturbed primary mass grave, and Lazete 2B a disturbed primary grave. A minimum of 165 individuals were contained in Lazete 2 of whom 158 died of gun-shot wounds. Again, blindfolds were also recovered with the remains. The third site at Pilica was very large, measuring 28 metres by 5 metres and 3 metres deep. There were a minimum of 132 individuals exhumed from that grave. Seventy-seven of these individuals had their hounds bound behind their backs, including one individual who had an artificial leg. The fourth sight, the four Nova Kasaba graves, contained 7, 19, 6, and 1 individual respectively. Ligatures were also recovered from 27 of the victims. And the individuals recovered from Nova Kasaba grave 2 were lying prone and others were sitting or in a kneeling position with 13 of the 19 having their hands bound behind their backs. Now, Dr. Haglund also explained the procedure once exhumed remains were taken to the morgue, that they were photographed there, passed through a fluoroscope, that the pathologist conducted their autopsies, and the forensic pathologists would assist in reconstructing the damaged bones and in determining the sex, age, and minimum number of individuals. That conclusions the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Haglund, I'd like to turn to the end of the summer of 1996. Were there some complaints from your professional colleagues lodged against the chief pathologist, Dr. Kirschner, as well as yourself?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And did the UN take up a study and panel -- an expert panel to review those allegations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now the individuals on the panel, were those people of high esteem and reputation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. They were from Canada and the United States, and I think there were two from England also.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, you have seen this document. It's D00329. If we can call that up. But -- in fact, actually, I'd ask that 65 ter 20008 be called up instead. That's the Prosecution version of the same Defence exhibit, except we have the B/C/S uploaded, and I believe the last time I checked the Defence also only had the English up there. So I won't readmit this document, but I will use it since there -- I will use the Prosecution version for the time being if that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's the same but with a translation, that seems to be preferable.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So if we could then have 65 ter 20008 displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Dr. Haglund, without getting into any details, could you briefly tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: These are individuals who are very well known in the United States, UK, and in Canada for the works they do. And I think they were -- oh, I'm getting the -- oh, I see. I should look at the English part here. I want to make sure ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just if you can tell us, is this -- is this the report that was created which documented the findings of this expert panel we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's start with Dr. Kirschner who is now deceased. Can you tell us who he was and what his role was in Bosnia in 1996?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, he would be in charge of the autopsy area, and then -- and overseeing the anthropologists that were in the laboratory also. But he left the country many times. He had a full-time job in Chicago and he was actually head of the -- that kind of work for the Physicians for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Was there -- perhaps we can just also clarify. Now, Dr. Kirschner, was he member of the expert panel or --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, he wasn't. He was a person that they were looking at.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. So there were some allegations against him. And was, in fact, the allegation -- the main allegation against him was that he changed some of the causes of death on some autopsy reports without consulting the pathologist who created them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Without consulting some of them. He was trying to make it more, I think, easy to put those in columns and that -- otherwise you'd have 400 plus individuals doing it. So he wanted to make it more clean, I think, and so that they could use a -- make better, you know, write a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you just give us an example?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, they were of -- of papers made so that the pathologist could put in all the kinds of things they wanted to. That -- what they had to do, and then they put extra stuff on them. Bob wanted to make -- apparently, he wanted to make the cause of death more of a general cause of death in many cases and not the ones that the pathologists wanted to do. Some of them he asked and some of them apparently he did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, when you refer to "Bob," are you referring to Dr. Kirschner?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Robert Kirschner, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now was it confirmed by the expert panel to have happened, that these changed were made without consultation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's -- that's -- that's what they questioned, and actually Mr. McCloskey took the -- all of the writings on how -- what the -- what the pathologists had done, and he went all over the world and -- to see if they needed to have their -- their writings changed or if they were -- if it was the same way it was. And then they would change it, and then he would go on to another country and find another people, so he went basically all to the -- I think there were 30, 30-some pathologists that we had from Turkey, England, United States, and all over. And that's -- he carried things around, but Mr. McCloskey, of course, didn't change anything. It was none of his business. He just took it to the pathologist.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And was this done before matters went to the oversight committee?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I believe they must have because it was -- it's in the -- it's in their report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can turn to page 10 in the English and B/C/S of this report. And if we take a look at the third paragraph under item B, opinion and comments of Dr. Vincent J. M. DiMaio. And it reads -- sorry, and -- and is Dr. Vincent DiMaio one of the experts sitting on the panel?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So he writes: "While Dr. Kirschner's actions had the potential to invalidate or at least taint the autopsy reports, the Tribunal prevented this by submitting the reports back to the physicians for their certification of cause and manner of death. Therefore, the panel feels no permanent injury to the validity of the reports was affected by the actions of Dr. Kirschner." Dr. Haglund, is this what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: All -- all of the people on that particular committee of -- of -- belive the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, the allegations that were directed towards you, were those upheld by the expert panel?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go over those allegations.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now there are approximately 17 individuals who were interviewed by the panel.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And four of them were critical of you. One of the criticisms come from Dr. Clyde -- sorry, from Clyde Snow. And if we could turn to page 4, please, in the report. And his criticism is found in item 5 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now he says -- if we just read the comment, he states -- states: "'Obviously sloppy science' was done. He felt at times it was Dr. Haglund versus UNTAES and mentioned the many bodies removed on one day. Dr. Snow stated in his opinion no more than 20 bodies should have been exhumed in a single day," and," he felt Dr. Haglund showed 'very poor judgement,' and it was lucky nothing had 'blown up' as a result of the procedures used." Now, before we get into those comments, can you tell us who Dr. Clyde Snow -- sorry, who Clyde Snow was and what his role was, if any, in the exhumations of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: He is a very well known anthropologist. I learned an awful lot from him. We were very good friends. But he had a lot of people from South America that he had -- had thought -- so they're children, and if they didn't like something then he would sort of protect them. He had nothing to do with the Bosnia diggings at all. He was in Croatia and he came to the grave-site once. However, he spent most of the time in the capital working with the people there so that he could -- they could give him information. He put it up on a computer so that they could work on that, so that -- that was for identifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So these comments that he makes, would they be in relation to the Ovcara site in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No. He was a -- he was saying it for everything. And it makes a difference how many -- how many remains you can take out in a day. It depends upon the kind of -- of grave you have. It depends on how intermixed and commingled the bodies are when they are in the grave. It has to do whether they are skeletalised or adipose -- where a lot of the cases in the deeper graves were. And so there were a lot of -- a lot of things you had to look at. And when I'd looked at the numbers of days we'd had, we never accepted the Ovcara grave. It's a different grave. But we never took out more than 12 -- 12 individuals in a day and in some -- at some places we only took four out in a day. It depended upon the kind of soil in the area that we were working at and, et cetera, and how deep the grave was and how the people had been put in. If the grave had been -- after the graves had been buried, that the individual then buried, then when the Serbs came back and dug those up with big backhoes that they would just go in blindly and pull out bones, and people, parts of them, dropping bones they left on top of the grave. Come and went away. Come back again and did some more. And so especially with the Lazete grave and somewhat with the Pilica grave we ran into that problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now you made an exception for the Ovcara grave. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The Ovcara grave, we -- I think we had a lot of problems not getting started early enough in the year. So we got in the rain and that was very hard, especially when you're dealing with 2 and a half to 3 metres and that soil is very -- it's very dangerous. The Lazete 1, I had to stop it because we knew there was an individual sticking out. We could not take it out. I wouldn't want anybody else to go in there because the sides were starting to crumble. It was very dangerous. And so then subsequently then people came afterwards and got the other 13, I think, individuals that we left there. But I made that clear in the report so that people would know that we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And, Mr. Snow, when he makes this criticism, how much actually -- how much time did he actually spend with you in Bosnia at the sites, the Srebrenica-related sites?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: About a half a day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could turn now to page 5 of the report and look at item 13. This is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- this is -- okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If you have something to say you can.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, that's all right. I leave the Ovcara grave. It's not a Srebrenica grave, so it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Item 13 on that page are comments by Dr. Dorothy Gallagher --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- and she's an anthropologist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: She says she saw problems in the field and in the lab. And stated that Dr. Haglund changed the autopsy reports and instructed her to do so. Dr. Haglund dictated too much speed in exhumation. The result was commingling, failure to associate body parts. Now Dorothy Gallagher, did she work on the Bosnia exhumations?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, on some of them. She had a master's degree, and they -- I don't believe in the majority of the people I -- look at -- I had over 70 or 80 people. We have four people crumbling. So -- I mean, these are the people in the graves and stuff, so --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just -- let's just address the comments she makes. Did commingling result from the way you removed bodies from the graves?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It would -- commingling, and that's when you have skeletal material and maybe the bodies would be -- had been maybe two, three times right on top of each other or part of it gone. And -- -- and, yeah, sometimes it could get commingled, but it was not as much on the way we took things out. When we knew that we were having -- or we had a hand or feet and they were skeletalised rather than, you know, try to leave -- move all those bones separately, we would put them all in a bag and tie them to the ulna and the radius. In the same way we would do the same thing with tying the feet, so that we would have all those feet and hand. But when you're dealing with that nasty grave like the -- the first grave that we did --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Cerska?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah. Cerska. That was in a -- water didn't run -- water ran through it because there were rocks and pebbles, and it got very, very hot. And within a year, a lot of those bodies were skeletalised already. And so you have rocks, metal -- and then, if there is spaces in between them, then you lose little bones that will fall through the cracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: And so those kinds of things made it a problem. You just have to deal with those problems. So ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Would you say that any such commingling comprised the determination of the cause of death or manner of death?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. If we can -- there was also a criticism from David del Pino?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And he's a Chilean anthropologist?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: He says: "Operations were halted when Dr. Haglund was away. Clothing was discarded at Dr. Haglund's command, even though some contained identification." Could you please comment on that criticism?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay. Some closing was left behind. If it was clothing that had any kind of thing that had any mail in there or anything that would lead to identification, we definitely took those. Okay. We didn't leave them in the grave. But we did lose some clothing that was separated from the bodies, et cetera. We left some of that, not very much, but we left some of it in the grave because we had just got rid of it when we got back at the laboratory. Because all that clothing and all those notes and stuff were gone through first to the Tribunal, and then everything was released to the -- the Bosnians so that they could work on the identifications. So the clothing would help, notes would help, photographs would help, that people would have them with them. And there was another part of your question, I think?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask some further explanation. You said: "But we left some of it in the grave because we had just got rid of it when we got back at the laboratory." That is a bit unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was -- this was basically a -- clothing that was not attached or with anybody else. It was not unique clothing at all. And anything -- some of that we left behind. We didn't take it to the laboratory because we'd got rid of it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What do you mean by "it was not unique clothing at all"? When is clothing unique?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, people that were in -- in Srebrenica, they didn't have a lot of clothes. They didn't go to a store to buy any. They were using a lot of old worn clothes that other people had worn and many people had the same kind of clothing. That's -- that clothing, if it wasn't unique, it wasn't going to help us identify someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But could you determine that on the spot how unique or not unique it was? I take it that you find --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because so many of the people had similar -- similar clothing, and it wasn't unique.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But was that -- how was it examined to what extent it was unique or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we took it out, we unfolded it, made sure that it was nothing in the pockets or anything. And then you look around and see a lot of the other clothing was just the same. It wasn't unique enough to add. If it -- some of the -- in -- some of the clothing had patches and things like that, and that's very important because the families had to sew those on and that was very important to identification. It was -- some very little clothing was left behind, and I think it was just a little bit at Lazete. I don't think that we had other clothing that was left anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said "we had to get rid of it."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't have to get rid of it, but it was -- it was like were we going to take some stones or rocks with us also? No, it wasn't unique to the identification of the individuals that we were moving out of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just to be clear, Dr. Haglund, was this clothing associated with any skeletal remains, be it --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, anything that was --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- bodies parts other otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Any -- any -- any piece of clothing that was wound around or close to a remains, we would not -- we would not leave it behind. It would always go with us. Some of it would be away from the bodies. I don't know if that's when the people got killed and there were some other stuff left up there on -- when the -- on the side of the road and they just threw it in the grave. I don't know. But it wasn't attached or on any individual, and it wasn't a unique sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now -- yes, the other criticism I had referred to is that operations were halted when you were away. Could you --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, they were --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- comment on that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was not because then another individual took his place. The name is slipping from me. It was a good friend.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Is that Mr. --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Pablo, Pablo, Pablo.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, Pablo Baraybar. So when I would leave a grave he was in charge. Period. And he didn't sit around and do nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the rest of the comments have to do with management. So I'm just going to leave those. Did you -- did anyone complain about your work in the morgue or your anthropological work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's look at the findings of the expert panel on those allegations.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we can turn to page 7 in the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I'll just read from the findings there: "The responses of the witnesses did not indicate any actual wrong-doing on the part of Dr. Haglund nor anything regarding the exhumations that jeopardised their scientific validity. The pathologists who were working in the morgue made no complaints about the exhumation of the bodies or the conduct of the anthropologists who were working in the morgue or at the grave-sites. Rather, it became apparent that the main problems with the exhumations were administrative and logistic. Whether real or imagined, there were concerns regarding international politics imposing a great deal of pressure on the teams to complete the exhumations quite rapidly. Even so, there was little real evidence the pace of the exhumations adversely affected the overall scientific quality. Along with the pathologists, the most experienced archeologists stated that the recovery of the bodies had been done adequately under difficult circumstances." Dr. Haglund, did you disagree with any of those conclusions?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now on page 8, if we turn to page 8 of the report, we see that the panel has made some recommendations. And under item 1, the first recommendation, they say, and I'll quote from there: "A few problems of administration or temporary lapses from a scientific ideal could not jeopardise the overall quality of the evidence and its interpretation at autopsy. Any prosecution of war crimes in Yugoslavia will be on firm scientific grounds. There are literally hundreds of war crime remains that were removed and interpreted by very scientifically sound methods." Again, Dr. Haglund, do you agree with that recommendation?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move on to the graves themselves, beginning with Cerska.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, were you the first one to arrive to do such a full exhumation of a grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, there were graves that archeologists did. I can't think of any contemporary mass graves that were dug up for -- in the United States. And most of it's -- and most of it's archeology. It's very, very old graves, hundreds of years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us in relation to the Cerska site, what were your conclusions about what had happened happened there, and if you could just explain that to us briefly?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay. This was a gravel road going uphill to Cerska, a small village. The -- the individuals were brought up there, I don't know if trucks or buses or whatever. They were lined up along the side of the road that sloped down to a small little creek, and they were shot, sort of a -- not just one in the head or something, that they just sort of be --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Are you referring to kind of a spray shooting method?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: A spray shooting, a spray shooting. And the people would fall over the edge or they would roll over the edge, and if they -- and many of them were shot many times over many parts of their body, and then, I think, if they were not -- not alive -- if they were still alive, they would go there and shoot them in the head. And then they would get another group and they would shoot them, and they would pile up all along the road for quite a -- for several yards.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now in your report - and that's 65 ter 4548 at page 9 of the English and B/C/S - --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, "several yards," what do I have to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was -- was 30 -- I have the -- I have the size of it in here. I have to look it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't need the precise details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But several yards could be anything between 2 yards and 2.000 yards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's more like probably 30 yards maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in your report where you discuss the scene and the circumstances of death and burial, you provide that the movement of the soil to bury the bodies had been accomplished using earth-moving equipment. Can you tell us how arrived at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, you can see across the -- the road went -- had been cut to a sort of a hill-side, and then the bank continued. So they used a -- probably a bank -- a hole that would dig it out of across the way, so that you would have a big bite out of the other side of the road, all that gravel, and then they would dump it on -- on top of the remains. So that was there. And then, of course, a -- the cartridges, most of the cartridges were strung along -- were in -- were in actually little piles where the people were standing where they -- uh -- with the -- um -- spit out the top part of a cartridge. And they would be there. Some of them also would be across the street, across the road. But then a lot of carts had driven up there for the year from the time that they were killed, and we didn't -- we didn't get them all, but we got -- we picked those up when we were first there, actually -- when they first went, Jean Paul, when they went.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: How could you tell that the fill that was used was not dug out with a shovel?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Not a little shovel, no. It was a big shovel. It was a mechanical one. There was just too much to spread along 30 yards if you were just doing that with a shovel. I don't think that they did that. I know that they didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: I think they didn't do that. I know they didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you could see the -- where -- when these -- they dug in, you could see the spaces. They would take out a hunk and you could see how broad that space was when they removed it so it wasn't a little shovel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you mean the pattern --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which was created by the shape of the mechanic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You saw it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- bucket.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, bucket. That's correct. That's correct. That's a bucket. I'm sorry. And you had the same thing at Lazete and it was impressed in the soil so that you could see it. You knew exactly how wide it was and you measured it, first of all, and I think they found -- they found the machine that did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the regularity of the intervals in between were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you have spoken a little bit about the cartridges that were found. And in your report you discussed how that goes to your conclusion that the victims were shot. Was there anything in the graves themselves that led you to conclude that these individuals were shot?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, when you get -- when you look at them you can tell that they had been shot. Okay? But it's a hole in a tunnel following the bullet. But a lot of -- a lot of cartridges also were spread along with -- when the -- when the gravel was took up -- taken off from the opposite side of the road, they also picked up then some of the cartridges, and they fell -- they fell in the grave also, so we had those spread out amongst the gravel that had been put on top of the bodies. The cartridges were in there, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: How about in and around the -- in and around the body parts and the remains in the graves, was there any other evidence that existed that led you to believe they had been executed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, the executions were mostly all the stuff was -- there -- some was in it, but it was brought in by a machine. The actual -- the kicking out as a cartridge kicked out as they were shooting, that is automatic rifles, that would be in a little area right around where the individual who was shooting them. It would shoot out the side and it would pretty much get in one little area, and another little area where the other person was standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you find ligatures, then, on some of the individuals in the Cerska grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I believe so. Let's see if I have that. Yeah. I -- there are some ligatures in there. Yes. For Cerska we had 24 ligatures that were in place, individuals' hands were tied behind their back. Actually, it was wired behind their back. They used wires as ligatures. And then 24 were in place. And then another 24 were associated with the bodies. Maybe one ring of that was on there. At one time they would have a ring around -- a wire around this -- this wrist and another on a wrist and then they would tie it together with another piece. So maybe you would just have one there, and then the other ones when -- when it would turn into a skeleton and then it would roll off. So it wasn't right on it but it was lying right by the limbs that usually on the -- on the wrists. It was lying by them. But in all -- in all total, we had -- what did we have? Forty-eight. Forty-eight wired [Realtime transcript read in error "wider"] ligatures.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Were those ligatures found in one place in the grave or were they dispersed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They were dispersed all over because as they dispersed the gravel over the tops of the body, they picked up the -- the -- some of those and -- some of the wire, when they had the bodies or -- they had wire, other wire. Now, were you asking me -- could you ask me that question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yeah. I just wanted to know whether the ligatures found on the individuals, were those individuals dispersed throughout the grave --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- or were they clustered in one part of the grave?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No. There was not one group of people that had their hands wired behind their back. There was people all along the side of the road that they had lined up. So there -- yeah, there were these ligatures of -- wired ligatures were spread on individuals all over the -- the grave. You'd find maybe two or three people that did not have their hands wired, they didn't have a ligature, but you'd find another one or two that had had ligatures.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask for one clarification in the transcript, line 14 of the previous page, 29. You are recorded as having said "Forty-eight wider ligatures," but I think you said "Forty-eight wired ligatures"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were no -- there were no clothed ligatures. These were all wired and this -- and again Cerska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Perhaps this time I have made a poor estimate of how much time I need. I will certainly need about 20 minutes, 15 to 20 minutes more. I understand I've already used up 50 minutes, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. With 15 to 20 minutes. You asked for one hour, I think if I'm --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I just wanted to notify you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- that I may go over my time estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you seek leave to go over your time estimate.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood. We'll take the break after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Mr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time. In the Rule 92 ter motion for Witness RM253, which was filed confidentiality on the 12th of April, the Prosecution sought, inter alia, the admission of five associated exhibits into evidence. Now, during the testimony of that witness, on the 11th and 12th of June, the Prosecution did, however, not tender three of these associated exhibits, namely the documents bearing 65 ter numbers 28898, 28900, and 28901. And the question of the Chamber is whether the Prosecution can confirm the withdrawal of these three documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll have an answer back very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P1481 displayed and page 3 -- that's page 3 in the hard copy version of that book and page 9 in e-court. I think if we can only have one of those images displayed, it would be a bit clearer.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay, Witness, can you tell us what it is we're looking at here?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, you're looking at the road of -- of the -- that the Cerska grave was on. I'd not seen this before. But you have July 95th. There is no digging in that area at that time and no -- once you look at 27th of July, 1995, and you can see that a lot of disruption of the soil and the gravel and that had taken place sometime between those two -- two times.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what can you tell us about the disturbed area that we see on the right-hand side, which is labeled 27 July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, what you see is what -- what I explained earlier, that was the gravel taken from one side of the road and spread over the other side of the road to bury the remains.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you a little bit, Madam Hasan. Mr. Haglund, at page 32, line 6, you are recorded as having said, "I'd not seen this before." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You had not seen it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not this one, no. These two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, when you say "I had not," do we understand that you are seeing this for the first time or you saw it sometime back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the first time I've seen this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: First time you seen it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, Dr. Haglund, just to follow-up on that question, you didn't see this at the time you were working there, but is it correct that I had shown you this image yesterday during proofing?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And was that the first time then you saw it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So taking a look at the image on the right-hand side, you said that this shows us what you were speaking about yesterday. Can you tell us on which side we see the grave on -- and what we see on the other side of the road? And --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- tell us which is which.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well the -- on the -- the left-hand side you have a long white streak across, one's the -- I think maybe the southern side. I am not sure whether it's southern or north. But on that side of the -- of the slope is -- is the grave, and then on the right-hand side is where the gravel was taken from.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now this -- [Microphone not activated] This Chamber has recently received the names of individuals who have been determined to have come out of the Cerska grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, these names were provided by Witness RM254.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: These, in the ICMP list of DNA matching reports, which is Exhibit P1727, are individuals bearing the case ID number CSK-30, CSK-32, CSK-36, CSK-101, and CSK 116. Dr. Haglund, are those case IDs familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They are from the Cerska grave, but when did you get this information because I would have thought that there was a lot more identified since the time that the graves were dug?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: That's correct. There have been more identifications, but I'm just specifically referring to these particular --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- individuals. Now those designations, where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, if you got out the map we could probably -- if you had the number --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: -- we could tell where they were buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- I don't mean where they were in the grave, but I mean just the designation itself. Was that something that your team had assigned to the remains as they were exhumed or ...

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: You mean the --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The numbering, the numberings, yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, that's how we numbered. We'd have a C on that and we had a number as -- as the time we took them out. We started with 1, 2, 3, 4, and went up to 150, and those are the numbers from that grave. All the graves have a -- a couple of -- two notes to -- you know, like Cerska, PL, C -- CS or whatever we had, and that would be tallied to the individuals that were in that particular grave.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And for Cerska it was CSK --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- and then the number following?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: There is a photograph, Your Honours, that I'd like to show the witness. It has -- was not previously on the 65 ter list, and it's photograph a photograph that's listed in the photo documentation log which is one of the annexes to Dr. Haglund's Cerska report. So it's a volume 2. And I've just pulled that photograph. It's -- has a provisional 65 ter number 29131, and I'd seek leave to add that one photograph to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Then could we have 65 ter 29131 displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And in the meantime, Dr. Haglund, were photographs of the remains taken as a regular practice?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. All of them would be photographed before they were moved.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Looking at the photograph that you see before you, can you tell us what it is that we see here?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, you see number 30. It's lying head down. You see the cranium and -- it's a skull, actually, down at the right -- right end. And then we see the -- the legs -- actually, right about -- right about the knee level is the number 30 is and then you see the legs go out, and you can see the feet and the -- the lower legs at the left end of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So that would be -- that's the remains of CSK-30?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And what about the marking 32?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Thirty-two. There is one right underneath here. You can see some of the clothing. It looks like probably the shoulder where the 32 is, but it's not as well delineated at this time. Once we get the other remains out then we can delineate the one below better.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. And we don't see it very well on the screen but there seems to be another individual's remains behind 30, marked 31?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct. That's further up the hill.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So the markings 30 and 32 correspond to the individuals that the Chamber has heard about. Now I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please explain the origin of these plastic bags we see here on the -- on the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where the -- what was the origin? We brought these -- we brought these with them. As I was telling you, hands and feet, and that would be put in those bags or tied to the -- the ulna and radius to keep them with that individual. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And they are now on this picture located where you found the body parts --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- you have put into the plastic bags; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is where the hands or feet would be or something that was broken or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would offer 65 ter 29131 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 29131 receives number P1830, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Dr. Haglund, in Krstic - I'm moving now onto another grave, the Lazete grave - you explained that because of the rainy weather conditions you weren't able to determine whether 2A and 2B, the two graves, were actually two separate pits or a single one. Can you tell us whether the weather conditions at that time had any impact on your ability to remove all the bodies from -- from the grave, and in particularly Lazete 2B which was the disturbed one.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I believe that that was the whole area that had been -- the whole -- whole thing had been made into a -- actually, a -- a -- a -- they dug all along the whole thing and then they put a pile of bodies in it and then they would cover it up and then they would have another one [indiscernible]. The Lazete 1 was a one -- one pile of bodies. There was nothing connected to them going to the next one, okay? The next one was the second one, that is Lazete 2, that is the one that had been robbed of remains trying to remove the remains from the grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question to you, Dr. Haglund, was whether the weather conditions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- at the time had an impact on your ability to remove the bodies from the grave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was various -- we had a three-week hold-out and it started to rain. The grave was 2 and a half to 3 metres at some point. It was filling up. We started digging along side of -- of where we were digging so that the water would go in -- in that area and then we'd pump it out, but that really didn't work. It was raining too hard. We'd finished the Lazete 1. We were almost finishing the Lazete 2, but that's what I explained earlier. It was -- there was so much water and that -- it was dangerous for people to be down there and we saw that one leg sticking out. We knew there was something there. We left it in the report so that people could come back later on when they did and got them, but it was too dangerous to put people down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Dr. Haglund, you refer to Lazete 1 and 2. Am I correct that you're referring to the different -- the two collections of bodies that you found that in your report are designated as Lazete 2A and Lazete 2B --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now we've talked about Cerska and Lazete. Dr. Haglund, did you also oversee, then, the exhumations and examinations of the remains from the sites of -- at Pilica and Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't always there at the laboratory, but the -- the digging, yes. The removal of the exhumations, yeah, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Did you prepare reports of your findings for each of those --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- sites?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, you have them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you testified as an expert witness about those reports in the prior trials before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd offer those reports, those expert reports into evidence at this stage pursuant to Your Honours' 19 July 2013 direction that the Prosecution refrain from tendering the underlying supportive materials. I accordingly offer into evidence only volume 1 for each of the expert reports, those being the main reports. And they are 65 ter 4548, 65 ter 4553, 65 ter 4559, and 65 ter 4558.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to admit that I am a bit surprised that those reports were not listed as associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were listed as non-associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right. And I don't think they are sufficiently dealt with today during the examination, so they want to have it in the evidence they should deal with them much more and much thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: -- the during lying reports were the basis of the entirety of the Krstic testimony. Dr. Haglund goes through site by site discussing his findings there. I didn't go over that same information here again today because it exists there on the record. The reports were provided -- were -- I mean, notice of the reports that we sought to admit them were in the 94 bis notice, and subsequently in the 92 ter motion I believe that motion also specified that the Prosecution would be tendering the expert reports of Dr. Haglund.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any response to this, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, to be -- I don't know by heart what is in 92 ter. I had other stuff to read. But I would maintain my objection. I think it's a -- and you can see in the Krstic trial, it's not dealt with. Those reports in --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In any length, and today it was just discussed with the doctor about this report from San Antonio commission. They had time to deal with the expert reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. So notice was provided in the 94 bis notice that the Prosecution sought to admit those reports. That was the whole point of calling Dr. Haglund to come here for cross-examination on those very reports. In the 92 ter motion at paragraph 12, we did specify that the Prosecution, in addition to the associated exhibits, will tender Dr. Haglund's expert reports. All of Dr. Haglund's expert report were admitted in the Krstic case. I didn't list them as associated exhibits because they were going to go in in any event pursuant to our 94 bis application.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excerpts of transcript of testimony of Dr. William Haglund from Prosecution versus Krstic case is one of the associated exhibits. You've -- the rest of the reports associated, exhibits with this testimony, they should be notified as associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have no problem to have it admitted as associated exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were not exploring all of them because they were not list as associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were listed as non-associated exhibits --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which would require you as much to explore it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but I expected them to go through them and then I would -- I would know where they are going. Which way. Then I would be -- I am --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- taking notes and be able to cross on those topics --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- not just to be dumped on us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided to MFI for the time being the -- the documents. And Ms. Hasan, we will further consider the matter after cross-examination. Then, Madam Registrar, 65 ter 04548 receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1831, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is MFI'd. The second one was 04558. Yes, but you listed them in this way, I think, or did you not? Okay. Then 04553?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P1832, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is MFI'd. 04558.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or 9 is -- no.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P1833, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number P1834, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is also MFI'd as are all the others, also the previous one. Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Then there is the associated exhibits. Your Honour, should I read them one by one or the entire list? And just for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just for your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of them may meet some of the concerns of Mr. Lukic, because 04553 is also on the list of associated exhibits, Mr. Lukic. So you said, Well, I would have expected them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would withdraw our objection to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To this one. Then P1832 is admitted into evidence. The other three remain, keeping the status of being MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Associated exhibits further.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: The remaining associated exhibits, while they look like they are numerous, in fact, they are all photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are all photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not have objections to any of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar, could you already reserve a range of numbers for -- for 13, if I am not mistaken, associated exhibits and prepare a list then assigning the relevant P numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My math is getting worse, Ms. Hasan. Fourteen numbers should be -- a range of fourteen numbers should be reserved. Madam Registrar, that would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Numbers P1835 up and including P1848, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they are admitted into evidence and the specific assignment of numbers to the individual exhibits we'll find that on the list which Madam Registrar will then file. Please proceed -- or you have no further questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Ms. Hasan. Then, Mr. Lukic, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you first need your lectern, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's through the -- Mr. Haglund, once Mr. Lukic has found his lectern, he'll cross-examine you. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. And no surprise, you'll find him to your left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Doctor. Can we start? [In English] Can we start?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you are getting the translation because I put some questions before you and you did not answer. But at least you will not have a problem with me because I will speak the front language.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, your field of work is injuries on bones. You did not deal with injuries if they were conflicted on soft tissue; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I would only comment on bones. But I worked for 15 years in the medical examiner's office. I saw a lot of -- a lot of -- lot of flesh, yes. But yes, I'd only comment on bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, it was pathologists, doctors, who did the post-mortems. I am talking about Bosnia-Herzegovina and the graves that have to do with Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, the leader of the pathologists was Dr. Kirschner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also worked under Dr. Kirschner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct, in regards to the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to ask you briefly now about Cerska. Is it correct that in this grave the bodies were in different stages of decomposition?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the basis of scientific facts and findings, can you rule out the possibility that the bodies in this grave were buried at different points in time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, you told us that on some bodies ligatures were found in this grave and on other bodies ligatures were not found; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doesn't this fact also indicate that the bodies buried in this grave originate from various incidents?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, of the people -- the individuals that had the -- the wirings behind their back was all over the grave. Some were down deep, some were superficial, some were at one end, some were in the middle, some were the other end. It was all mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So according to you, the difference with regard to the degree of decomposition of the bodies and the fact that some bodies had ligatures and the others did not, does not allow for the possibility to conclude that the incidents in which these people lost their lives were different ones?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: You mean differently dumped in or something, whatever?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I meant killed at different times and then buried at the same place.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: They were buried the same time, same place. They would -- there is -- differential decaying of the remains depended upon how superficial they were in the grave, how -- how -- they had a lot of sun. The rocks on the top were warmer than the ones on the bottom, and that helped change the decomposition. Decomposition of the ones below were in better shape than the ones on the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Haglund, you asked a response to the previous question, "You mean differently dumped in or something, whatever?" And then Mr. Lukic said, "I meant killed at different times and then buried in this same place." And then you said, "They were buried the same time, same place." You were exclusively talking about burials, whereas the question was about when they were killed and perhaps where they were killed and whether they were buried in the same grave. You have not addressed it, that part of the question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. All the cartridges were strung along the whole side of the road. Very, very many of them. That's where they were shot. In fact, I believe there may have been someone else who knew about them and knew about what happened, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, your answer refers to evidence that made you conclude that many people were killed there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
