utterances.text: Now Mr. Lukic may want to know whether it also allows for a definitive conclusion that all of those buried were killed at that time there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's possible some of them had been killed somewhere else, but the majority of them certainly seemed like they were ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what makes you conclude that it was the majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you would see -- well, the levels -- I mean, when you have bodies tied up with each other, tied up with the ones all this side and down below and that, nobody would put those in and -- and put their arms out -- and under the next person and the leg under another person when they were putting a new group of people there. That's -- that didn't make sense to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you concluded from the position of the bodies that they were not superposed to bodies already there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the way in which they were found strongly suggests that they fell together in that grave at that point --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on like the other grave that were different piles of people and it could have been at different times, but this was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next issue with regard to this location, this is from your testimony in the Krstic case, P1828, page 12 in e-court. And it should correspond to the transcript page 3734. There you say in lines 9 and 10, and this is an adjudicated fact, you say that the age range in this grave was 14 to 50, and then you say that the two youngest were aged between 11 to 15. I would now ask you whether you would agree with me that in your reports you estimated the age and could not exactly determine this parameter?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That -- that's correct. We can't put on exact the -- exact age on these people. It's between what we think is the lower and -- and a older.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For each group and for each individual, you allowed an error of plus or minus one year of age; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I believe that's what they did on the -- I'd have to look at all them and review those again, but -- to look at the -- at the anatomy of the -- you would look at the -- of -- cases that are in the -- at the pathologist stuff that the -- at the archeo -- anthropologist gave to the -- if it's in there, I would have to look at that more. I haven't looked at that, so I could look at the other stuff and see where it's coming. But it's coming from the laboratory, not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you complete your last answer: But it's coming from the laboratory but not. What's not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, it's coming from there. I'm just looking here and seeing -- yes. It's in the -- it's in the -- the anthropologist gave it to the pathologist, and they included that in their report, which is fine. And I think I have some other diagrams and that on age in the reports, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with the following sentence, which I'm going to read out to you: [In English] "The final range given is the anthropologist's opinion of the individual's biological age and does not exclude the possibility that the true calendar age is outside the range given."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Exactly. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the specific case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, these estimates are sometimes without the framework because you did not have the standards for the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was not available to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's exactly right, too. We didn't have a lot of those. In the United States, we were a little closer. But in other countries, they don't do this kind of thing, and so, yeah, we didn't -- we'd -- these are not specific. There is always a plus or a minus on these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I then understand that the range you give in a country where you have more specific information about averages, that the range is smaller than the range --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you applied here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might be tighter, yeah. It may or not -- it may or may not be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you make it broader here then where you said you had not detailed information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think we went that far out but I think we did go a little far out than we would normally do like in the United States or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, "or something" is a rather broad --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do you have an answer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, I think these were the best that we could get at that time, and I think it was mostly based on what people knew when they were working with cases. It wasn't that far out or whatever it would be in United States or whatever, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you say on the one hand that if you have better information which allows you, if I understand you well, to a smaller range because there is less uncertainty about what you average --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On average would expect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you said, We didn't have that information in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least if you would not mind, I would rather conclude my question. You had less information about Bosnia. My question is whether you then also adapted the range which expresses some uncertainty in this situation compared to what you do -- would did in another situation such as in the United States?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we used pretty much what we did at home, I think, I guess when you really think about it. And as you get old -- as person gets older, then it gets wider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I can imagine that a one-year range doesn't apply when we are talking about people of 55 years of age, and then, of course, for youth it's quite different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that goes beyond my question, that in a different age group you would deal with that differently, because my question was focusing on, of course, this group of youth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. What -- what we -- we'd look at when the bones, the ends of the bones, the epiphysis is getting solid with the rest of the bone, and there we have -- it works better on younger people because we're looking at the epiphyses connecting solidly with the -- with the bone, for instance, at the end of the humerus. We have a couple of places where the bone is adhering to the rest of the bone and it takes a while to do it. When you have that, you can see the little -- the little crack if it's not fully attached. You -- it's easier to get a smaller -- to get an easier age when they're younger and get older it's -- I don't know if I'm done answering your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that you say that the development of the bone becoming far more soft, as in early youth --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to at a later stage --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- becoming harder, that that doesn't depend on, for example, the average length of people in a certain community or a certain population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that for that reason you had this relatively independent measurement. Could I urge you to be very precise in your answers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so that we fully understand --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what the basis for your opinions was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Lukic, if there was one thing still puzzling me from one of the previous answers. If you would give me just a second to find it again. You were asked at the time -- and I'm referring to page 45, line 3 or -- and 4. You were asked: "You also worked under Dr. Kirschner; is that right?" Your answer was: "That's correct, in regard to the autopsies." Now, a few lines before that you said it was pathologists, doctors, who did the post-mortems. Now, I'm a bit confused about the difference between autopsies and post-mortems, whether it's the same or whether it's different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the same. Well, then you said it was the doctors who did the post-mortems. At the same time, you said, when asked whether you worked under Dr. Kirschner, that you worked under him. You said that's correct in regard to the autopsies, but you did not perform the autopsies. So how did you then work under him in regard to the autopsies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was -- it was getting other pathologists in for him when he was gone and those kinds of things and nothing to do with the actual autopsies, but I'd do things for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you -- you understood the question whether you worked under Dr. Kirschner is whether you performed your job which would then enable the pathologists to do the post-mortems or the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you understand by working under. The question was a bit unclear, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Doctor, with regard to Cerska --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could please see 1D1159. And that's the transcript from the Tolimir trial, your testimony. We need page 74, which corresponds to page 9173 of the transcript, and we need lines 16 to 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I'm going to read this out to you: [In English] "Q. Can you tell us in the orders and the documents you found were preserved as part of the general collection, documentation? "A. That, I think, probably would have been preserved, I'm not sure. Many of the documents on bodies of the -- the identification documents and that -- that were turned over to the group that was trying to identify these people ..." [Interpretation] So we are talking about documents. Is it correct that in Cerska with practically every body you also found the personal papers or documents of those persons?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, not at -- not that many. I think I probably have it in here somewhere in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I just reviewed some of your reports cursorily, and I think that there are really many identification documents connected to this one. However, do you know now what happened with the identification documents from this location that you collected? Where did they end up?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The identification material was given over with the remains to the Bosnian so they could do the identifications. However, prior to any -- any things we found, paper then that -- the Tribunal would look at them first to see if it was important for them to have, and if they thought it was they took them and they have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "the Tribunal," you mean the OTP; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now ask you something brief about Nova Kasaba, though that is not even in our indictment, but just in order to understand the -- the methodology of your work. You described some bodies that were found in sitting or kneeling positions and that they were in those positions in the graves. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. The second grave was the one that most -- that stood out the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you want to say that they were buried in such positions, upright position, or that their legs were bent or were they turned on one side?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: There is -- there are photographs in the report that shows what was happening. People were bent over like this and they were shot in the back of the head. Some of them had sprawled out when they had fallen over after they had been shot, but you can see those in the photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you now about the grave-site number 4 in Nova Kasaba. Would you accept today the possibility or the likelihood that this one person in the fourth grave -- it's one person; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you accept the possibility that this person was killed at some different point in time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't think the person was killed. It looked like it was an elderly gentleman. He was lying on his back. Lying out just on -- like we would bury somebody. There were no -- he had not been shot. We found no other exterior wounds or anything, so I don't believe that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could I also urge you to be very precise in your questions because if you said at some different point in time, it's totally unclear to what you refer. Certainly different from when he was found, but do you refer to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are other three graves --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and then Nova Kasaba location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's exactly what I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for not being precise enough. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for a break. After the witness has left the courtroom, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. Mr. Haglund, we'll take that pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- in response to your request regarding Witness 253, we are withdrawing those exhibits. But thank you for reminding us. Those exhibits are not needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Yes. That was the documents related to Witness RM253.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, the Prosecution informed me that your health is somewhat precarious, and if you believe that you would need a break or some rest, please do tell us.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the break, we were discussing Nova Kasaba and the fourth grave-site there. Would you agree with me that you could not determine that the other three grave-sites that we talked about came into the existence at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I couldn't tell the same time of these graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we shall look briefly at Lazete, Lazete 2A and 2B. Inter alia, blindfolds are discussed with regard to this.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have these blindfolds been preserved and do you know where they are kept today?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I believe some of them -- I think maybe all of them at one point had been taken to the Tribunal. I don't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Krstic case it was mentioned on page 44 in e-court, corresponding to page 3766, that you found one skeleton outside the grave and that you buried it. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. In the assessment time we were looking at the graves, there was one on top of the -- a bit away from the grave. But in order to preserve that and keep it there and the dogs not getting it, we -- we did bury it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now something brief about Pilica and Branjevo farm. You mention 170 body parts. Do you know and can you tell us how many of the 170 body parts are individual bones or fragments of bones?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It's both. Sometimes it could be a leg, sometimes it could be an arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there parts or fragments of bones?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, some.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many, how many bone fragments?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't think we counted all of the fragments. It may be very small. But all the other bones we did save, and when we gave up the bones as well as the bodies, we were hoping that -- and they have matched some of them with DNA through the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Popovic case you were asked something, and I will present it to you now to ask you whether you would agree with the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So to that effect we need 1D1158. We need page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is your testimony in the Popovic case. And this has to do with the big grave-site which was only partly filled; correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll need lines 19 to 21, please. You were asked the following there: [In English] "Q. Okay. And were you able to determine whether this grave had -- had been disturbed in some way? "A. Not definitively, in my opinion."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Which one -- which one are we here at now? What grave are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we are talking about Pilica, the Branjevo farm. Would you agree with this, that you could not provide a final conclusion as to whether the grave had been disturbed in some way or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's true at that time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask, then, the witness whether it's not true anymore now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were photographs that were -- fly-over photographs that showed the grave was being dug at after the fly-overs were shown to the UN. There are three -- three photographs that were taken when the bodies were out on the -- on the field and the grave of -- being bodies put in. The second time there were oversights that the bodies were being dug up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This was unknown at the time when you gave your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how did you learn about this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- after you gave your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw here a year or two later, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the photographs were provided to you by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I may have seen them here. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you know exactly which photographs were shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were three of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I understand your answer well that on the basis of what you've seen since you grave your testimony --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that is there a likelihood that on the basis of new material that one could come to a different --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- conclusion. That the conclusion could be more certain in either one way or another.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when you saw those photographs? What year was that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Probably 19 -- late, maybe late 19 -- maybe 1997 or something like that. I hadn't seen them around the times that the exhumations and the -- and, actually, when the reports were written. So it's probably past 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now I am confused a bit, because you said during the testimony in the Popovic trial you didn't know about these photographs. Now you say it was probably 1997 or 1998. But your testimony in Popovic was given in March 2007.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. It was later than that, then, because I didn't know about it at that time. I don't know when they came out. I -- I can't remember exactly when I saw them, but certainly it wasn't at that time at -- that testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it you don't know when you saw them first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for these photographs that you are telling us about now, they are not part of your report; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I happened to see them. I don't know quite where I saw them. It might have been on the -- on the web somewhere or something. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. These photographs, can one see whether the bodies are being buried or whether they are being exhumed in these later photographs? On the basis of what do you conclude that the bodies were not being exhumed rather than interred?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, there were different times. But -- we could see the bodies that were killed out on the field. You could see those from the first -- the first piece. The second one looked like the grave was being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was -- this was later, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if we invite the witness to comment on photographs, then, at least we would have to know what photographs exactly we are talking about and whether there were any bodies visible on the ground. Because if it's just the grave, I would say you can't exhume anyone if it's not buried before. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can add somebody in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- if somebody was not there before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then, of course, we would have to know what we are talking about if you're asking the witness to comment on matters he has apparently not thoroughly examined. At the same time, I have no problem in you testing the credibility and reliability of the witness in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I don't know which photographs the witness is talking about either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither do I.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you deal with calibres?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Calibres?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Calibres of weapons --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- that were used to kill people.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, the cartridges were given to the -- to the Tribunal, and they had experts that looked at those things. Not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the Serb forces at the time used 20- and 30-millimetre machine-guns to stop the break-through of the column from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As an anthropologist, would you confirm that these calibres - 20 and 30 millimetres, that is - can dismember bodies?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't think I'd want to -- to make that kind of -- of -- of -- of -- I think that other experts would have to do that, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Fair enough. Thank you. [Interpretation] Today, my colleague, Ms. Hasan, asked you about the report of the oversight commission. Now I am going to dwell on that report. You said to us today that about 70 people worked with you and that four persons complained.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's -- that's what the -- it says, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not all 70 were interviewed; is that right? Seventeen persons were interviewed. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yeah. It was a selected group for some reason, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when you testified in the Krstic case, were you aware of the judgement passed by the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I am not sure of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time when you testified in the Krstic case, because the judgement was passed before you testified in the Krstic case, so my question is: When you testified in the Krstic case, did you know that a judgement had been passed --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: In Rwanda.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in Rwanda?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think I might have been aware of that, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, your question may just be a little confusing. You say: "At the time when you testified in the Krstic case, because the judgement was passed before you testified in the Krstic case ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The judgement in Rwanda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In front of the Rwanda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which judgement are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Rutaganda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That is not clear from your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Because Ms. Hasan dealt with two different judgements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please help me out. The evidence given by this witness in the Krstic case was when exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Krstic case was 2000, I think, but I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I see that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Hasan is going to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, prior testimony is 29th of May, 2000. I see that. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll go back to that later. I would just like to ask you the following: When you testified in the Krstic case, you were aware of the investigation that was taking place in San Antonio - is that right? - because you testified there before testifying in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay. If that's true, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the Krstic trial - and that is part of our case today - the Prosecutor suggested that only one or two colleagues objected to your work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1828 is the reference, on page 3760 of the transcript. In e-court it's page 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay. That's what it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However -- actually, more than one or two young colleagues complained about you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think there might have been up to seven. It wasn't over that, but it could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, the colleagues who complained are not exactly young colleagues. They are men and women of your age, approximately; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think a lot of them -- or most of them were younger than me. One of them I know was my age, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to fully understand that, we would have to know your age.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm 70 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're 70 years old. Because the CV doesn't give your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was criticism of your work based only on the work in the mortuary or was it also based on your anthropological work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, there was anthropological work in the laboratory and in the -- in the exhumations, both places. The place -- people had worked in both places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So was their criticism in view of your anthropological work as well as archeological work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Of my -- you're saying two -- two things of -- could you repeat that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the criticism pertain both to your anthropological work and your archeological work in the cases that you worked on in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Anthropology, I'm not a -- I'm a -- I'm an anthropologist. They didn't do -- I didn't do any archeology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Lukic, that I understand what you're -- if I read from your testimony, which you said you reviewed recently, I see the following question - and I'm referring to page 37, 60: "Also at the end of this very long summer, did one or two of your young colleagues have some criticism regarding your supervision of the archeology work?" And your answer was: "Absolutely, yes. "Q. What was that about?" Well, then, you said something about the quality and the pace of work. But there, at least, your answer suggests that you supervised archeological work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of the people were archeologists and some of them were anthropologists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you supervising archeological work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, they were doing digging but not -- we were not doing digging like the archeologists did. We did digging like we would do to recover remains, to identify, to find out -- they're dead and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you said a minute ago, "I'm an anthropologist."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "I didn't do any archeology," which was a bit of a sloppy expression perhaps for: In my position as an anthropologist, I only supervised the work of archeologists but I didn't do that work myself. That is what you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- intend to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'd never gone -- done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I'm just asking you whether that would be a more precise phrasing of what you intended to answer to the question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the criticism presented before this oversight commission had to do with the work of the pathologist, the supervisor, Dr. Kirschner?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. Much of that was dealt with about Dr. Kirschner, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The criticism also pertained to the autopsy reports; right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's what it was mainly about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to ask for something in e-court. Although this is D329, a Defence exhibit, and the Prosecution uploaded the B/C/S version, that is 2008. That's the ERN number. And we would like to have the following displayed in e-court: RM2008. At least for the B/C/S version if it's possible to separate the two, if not -- [In English] 65 ter 20008.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] it is clear to us what we are discussing; isn't that right, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: The -- yes. And all the people there basically were anthropologists, but they may have had classes in archeology -- no. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us that there were experts there from Canada, America, and the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes. And from South America and from Honduras, from -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this commission, I mean -- on this committee, rather, there were people from Canada, the US, and the UK. However, you will allow me to say - and you will agree with me - that representatives from the UK were not present. At least here they have been registered as absent.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I have no idea of how they put that together. I have no idea of who was there. Only the -- only the individuals that were there at the time. I don't know who was there or not there, whatever. I had no -- I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the report itself, it was noted that the interviews were not recorded either in video or audio or using video or audio technology. We see that on page 2, III.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I saw that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Roman numeral III, please. That is not being challenged. We can see that from the report itself. What I am interested in is whether a written record was kept of these interviews. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: You have to ask the people that -- that did this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But the question to you was: Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You -- I couldn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know the individuals had known of the people who were doing this, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was not the question. The question was: "What I am interested in is whether a written record was kept of these interviews. Do you know about that?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if you read it, you'll find out they didn't keep anything. And if that's the last time I recall reading it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was again not the question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- what is written in the report. But do you know if any records were taken of these interviews?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, then. No, I don't know anything about that at all. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 3 of this report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I nevertheless return to the same issue. You say you don't know anything about it. One of your answers was: "I think if you read it, you'll find out that they didn't keep anything."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said that earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you formed an impression or whether they did or not on the basis of the report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it's clear to me. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We need page 3 of this document, both versions. We need Roman numeral IV. That is "Background Information."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that, yeah. Kind of hard to read it here. That helps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was stated that there was a potential conflict, if not a real one, between the UN personnel and the Doctors Without Borders personnel in terms of cause and manner of death. Now, the conflict on the ground, was it overcome?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If counsel could just clarify the involvement of Doctors Without Borders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there is a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I misspoke. Doctors for Human Rights, Physicians for Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That, Ms. Hasan, is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's the bottom part of this paragraph that starts: "There was also a potential, if not real ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, it was mainly about Mr. Lukic misspoke that you were responding to or is there anything else you would like to be explored prior to --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, it's just that Doctors Without Borders wasn't involved at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. Perhaps it's wisest to phrase your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we see here at the bottom of this paragraph it was stated that there was also a potential, if not real, conflict between the UN and PHR personnel as well as variations on legal opinion for cause and manner of death. First of all, let me ask you whether this commission properly understood the problem?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I am not really aware of what -- what went on with that. I really -- I wasn't aware of that. I see it here, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were on the ground. In your view, was there this conflict between you as the representatives of UN -- you were a representative of the UN, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So was there a conflict between you as the representative of the UN and the personnel of Physicians for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude, then, that this part of the report is wrong?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, it may be right. Other people might be involved. I have no idea what their problems were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: In fact, the report says that there is a potential, and it says "if not real, conflict," but there certainly is no conclusion that there is a conflict. It's an observation made based on the preceding sentences which discuss the professionals coming from different nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And therefore, I think, Mr. Lukic is entitled to ask whether the witness has any knowledge about the existence of a conflict. Even if the report says there is a potential conflict, then Mr. Lukic is fully entitled to ask such a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I was simply objecting to the representation that the panel found there was a conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The panel is working on this background information and [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of their findings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it's clear from the question that Mr. Lukic used exactly the words from the document we see on the screen. Page 71, line 2, that "there was also a potential, if not real, conflict."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: May if I, Your Honour, and then at line 10, the question is, "Can we conclude, then, that this part of the report is wrong." And he's talking about a conflict existing, an existing conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not fully consistent, it seems. In that respect, Ms. Hasan, I think you're right. At the same time, from what Mr. Lukic said earlier, there seems to be no intention to not reflect the content of the report. But the follow-up question was inconsistent with your previous question, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your view, why was your work criticised by people who worked with you or for you?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I -- there are some things I don't want to say. They were very good friends. A couple are very good friends with Clyde Snow. Look, you work with people, these things that are -- it's all right. That doesn't bother me. It doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was -- the question was not whether it bothered you but whether in your view -- whether you know the reason, not phrased perfectly, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but whether you know of the reason why people who worked with you or for you criticised you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether you're aware of the reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had one for one young man that did it. And actually, it was probably my fault. He was working in Rwanda with us and he came to Croatia -- and he came to Bosnia. His wife was pregnant. He needed money. I told him he should probably go home. He said, No, no, please can I stay. I said, Okay, you can stay, but you should really go home and he didn't so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what was your fault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't their fault. He just -- I think he just got tired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking you what you just said. What was your fault. You said "it was probably my fault."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I didn't send him home earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So his criticism of you would have been valid if it was your fault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was -- I was -- I was the person in charge so, that wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, so his criticism of you would have been valid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other people didn't agree with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking the question, sir, if you just answer mine. Would his criticism of you have been valid if it was your fault?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think it was just his perception.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is -- would you say it was your fault. I'm not asking about his perception. I am asking you about what you say. You say it was your fault. I saying if criticised you because it was your fault, therefore his criticism would have been valid, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was because he was tired. It's not that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I guess there is a difficulty here. Is it difficult to answer my question? I thought it was a very simple and straight-forward question. You're saying it was your fault and therefore he criticised you. Was he therefore justifiably criticising you? Just a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I should have sent him home earlier but I thought that may have been the problem, but I don't think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid that still doesn't answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, as I said the answer is going to be either a yes or a no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have to see his -- I'd have to see what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, listen to what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to take a more analytical approach as Presiding Judge of this Chamber. What exactly was his criticism against you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he thought we worked too fast. I think that was one of them. It's in here somewhere. And he -- he was angry about leaving some clothing behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So it was about the work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now you say yourself, I'm probably to be blamed for not sending him home which is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not about his work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was unrelated to his work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now your answer about why they would have criticised you, do we then have to understand your answer - although it was not very clear in that respect - that because he was overstressed perhaps due to the pregnancy of his wife and where you even thought that he should not continue to work, that he was in a mental state where he was criticising due to those circumstances rather than to have valid concerns about the way in which you operated? Is this how we have to understand your answer to the question why would they have criticised you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think in part probably he was very tired. I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It may be one thing. But I knew he was doing -- doing the work fairly well and he needed the money, so I let him do it. I wasn't -- I -- he'd never brought this up to me and so this is the first time I'd seen it or heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And why do you think you should have sent him home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he'd worked a long time in Rwanda and that, you know, he should have taken a rest. He could have come back or something but didn't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Despite the fact that he never brought this up to you, that it was too much for him --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but it was your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I just saw this in this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your colleagues who expressed their criticism criticised the procedure which you applied, among other things, as you just told us about this younger colleague of yours, that you worked too fast, that you destroyed some pieces of evidence or left them there? As, for example, items of clothing.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I think all this went by the people here that had to write this and they didn't think that was a problem, so -- and I didn't think it was a problem either. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, seeing the following questions, to what degree you agree with the report. But I will now ask you whether it is true that at the time when you worked in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were under constant pressure to finish the work?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I wasn't under constant pressure to finish the work. However, the -- we -- we were coming to the climate where it was going to be very rainy and we needed to finish the graves that we were going to do. We only did as many as we could and there were more that they wanted us to do, but we couldn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at 1D1158.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's your testimony in the Popovic case. We would need page 14 in e-court, which corresponds to page 8912 of the transcript. We would need lines 22 to 25, please: [In English] "Q. Were you under any pressure to get the work done and bring back evidence? "A. That was our goal for being there."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "So we had to maximise our time while we were there."

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this just a civilised way to formulate it? But isn't this precisely the explanation to the effect that everyone who was working on this project was under tremendous pressure?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't believe that. I think one of the problems is that they had never seen graves like this before. They'd never seen this many bodies, dead people and -- there. So they were used to doing maybe one case a month or -- and -- and this was hard on them, yes, in that respect. And in an -- in that respect probably -- I'm at a time I haven't talked about it anymore. I am just talking too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, apparently there were complaints about going too fast. There was a huge job to be done in not unlimited time. That's clear if --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we would move on, that would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Um-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You told us yourself today that most of the objections were directed at Dr. Kirschner for the reason that he changed the cause of death without consulting the pathologists who were conducting their own examinations. I would ask you whether that is the usual practice in the United States?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: It is not the usual practice in the United States, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you qualify the work as unprofessional? I mean, Dr. Kirschner's work, was he allowed to do this sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, if was back in -- in the United States, and they had younger people working, the person that was -- that was their boss would go through things and they might want to change things and they talk it over with the student pathologist and they would agree to it, and -- um, what Dr. Kirschner was doing. I think he probably talked to a lot of the individuals when they were there, but the -- the people that had left and he was putting this together, I don't know if -- what he did about other people. And a lot of people were possibly left out and had nothing to do or don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a long answer but not to the question. The question simply was: Was he allowed to do this sort of things; that is, to change reports without consultation. Now, apart from what consequences there are, whether circumstances would make it understandable why he would do it, do you consider that he was allowed to do it yes or no? That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think some of the pathologists allowed him to do that. He talked to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are changing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are changing the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am talking about without the consent --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of the pathologist to change their reports or conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, he shouldn't be doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct that the commission from San Antonio, that is to say the body which examined this case, found that the head pathologist had acted in a manner that was inappropriate?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I don't know where this is. I'm not sure. Could you show me it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will show you your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would need 1D1157, actually, page 40. Perhaps this is included in P1828.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is your testimony in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 40 in e-court. Just the one that we have on the screen right now. Transcript page 3762.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, perhaps I'm a bit lost, but this witness said that Dr. Kirschner was not allowed to do what he did. Now you put to him that the commission from San Antonio was of the same opinion. What -- what questions would you have in mind to further ask from that? The witness said that he was not allowed to do it. So therefore, let's -- apparently then, apart from that, of course, it's an opinion, but apart from that apparently the opinion is in line with the San Antonio commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only I asked on -- on page 80, line 17 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Is it correct that the commission from San Antonio ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Is it correct that the commission from San Antonio, that is to say the body which examined this case, found that the head pathologist had acted in a manner that was inappropriate?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the answer was: "I don't know where this is. I am not sure." And in the previous trial, the gentleman testified on this same issue differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he himself has testified that he considered that Dr. Kirschner was not allowed to do it, if you are talking about the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are not talking about the same, you have introduced it. Now it's -- it's -- whether the witness knows or doesn't know about the San Antonio commission, if he -- if you say, I'm testing the consistency of the witness in his answers in relation to what the committee reported, then please put it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were about to do that, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- testing his testimony in this and the previous case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I step back to some extent --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as you may have noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe you will let me do this. If I'm wrong, you will warn me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I think that we will understand each other at the end of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: That's correct. After I saw this, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What created confusion with me was that you said today that you didn't know where it was in the report. However, you do now remember that this mentioned in the report; correct? As I need that for my following question that I'm about to ask you.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Yes, yeah. Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please. Sometimes you start talking very early and the microphone is not working at that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer to what question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The microphone didn't pick up your question -- your answer, actually. And I think you said yes when I asked you whether you were aware of the conclusion of this commission in regard of that -- Dr. Kirschner?

utterances.text: Yes. I saw it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Was Dr. Kirschner interviewed by this panel?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I believe so. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As one cannot see from the report whether he was interviewed or not. He's not listed among the persons whose comments are provided. That's why I ask you whether you saw Dr. Kirschner being --

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: No, I would assume -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- invited and interviewed?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, I -- I just assume maybe he did, but that was maybe not good for me to say. No. I would have to read this and find out if he was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's break time.

utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whether -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: I'm a bit perplexed now. Is what you said in the Krstic case correct, that the rules and protocols had already been established, that everyone had been informed about these protocols, and that everybody abided by international standards in their work? Or was that not the case?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: I'm a little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I help you a bit, Mr. Lukic. The quotation was: "The administration of the work policies and protocols are established ..." That doesn't say anything if that was done in writing or orally or however we can understand what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.text: -- the witness said in the Krstic trial.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to go back to 65 ter 2008 [as interpreted]. utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, were they right when they supported Dr. Kirschner?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM HAGLUND
utterances.text: Well, it sound like they did. And they maybe felt that the change that Dr. Kirschner made didn't make a great deal of -- they understood it when they were going to write the -- when they were going to write the report, so I don't know what's in their minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain just briefly why I'm asking this. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.text: I give you time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I use the opportunity to deliver the Chamber's decision on two outstanding matters in relation to Witness Ekrem Suljevic. The first concerns the admission of the remaining two associated exhibits to his witness statement, and the second is a bar table request by the Prosecution relating to a range of documents. During the testimony of Witness Suljevic on the 11th of February of this year, the Prosecution tendered the witness's consolidated statement dated the 9th of February, 2010, which was admitted into evidence as Exhibit P889. Following the cross-examination of the witness and subsequent discussions among the parties the Prosecution, on the 13th of February, re-tendered a revised version of Exhibit P889 together with 19 associated exhibits. As the Defence had no objections to the admission into evidence of the revised version of this statement, on the 1st of March, 2013, the Chamber admitted it into evidence keeping the previously assigned exhibit number P889, and requested the Registry to replace the old version with a new one in e-court. On the 5th of March, 2013, the Registry filed an internal memorandum assigning provisional exhibit numbers ranging from P1097 up to and including P1115 to the 19 documents. On the 28th of June of this year, the Defence filed its submission with regard to the associated exhibits of Witness Suljevic, objecting to the relevance and authenticity of eight documents on the basis that the witness was not their author and therefore lacked any personal knowledge of them. With regard to the Defence's objection, the Chamber reiterates its reasoning in its oral decision of the 29th of October, 2012, that while it prefers that the witness through whom a document is tendered has personal knowledge of that document, this is not per se a requirement for admission as long as the document is sufficiently linked to the witness's overall testimony. Having reviewed the eight documents in question, the Chamber notes that there are investigation reports of various shelling incidents, analysing the impact of mortars or projectiles, an area relating to the exact same type of investigation the witness was primarily involved in while being a member of the anti-terrorist unit of the Sarajevo MUP. Moreover, all reports were generated by the same section in which the witness was working. In light of the foregoing, the Chamber is of the view that the eight documents are sufficiently linked to the witness's testimony. Before the Chamber proceeds to decide on the admission of the associated exhibits of Witness Suljevic, it notes one outstanding matter with regard to the document bearing 65 ter 10250, a MUP report on an explosion on Mustafa Behman Street on the 18th of July, 1995, which is also one of the 19 associated exhibits and currently MFI'd as P1110. This document was discussed with the witness in court on the 13th of February, 2013, and the Prosecution requested it to be marked for identification pending the completion of its translation, as currently only two pages out of a four-page report are translated in e-court. This discussion can be found at transcript page 8580. In line with the approach taken in the Tucker oral decision of the 22nd of November, 2012, the Chamber considers nine documents to be an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness has testimony and therefore admits exhibit numbers P1098 through P1101, P1109, P1110, P1112, P1114, and P1115 into evidence as associated exhibits to Witness Suljevic's statement. With regard to 65 ter number 10250, which was provisionally assigned exhibit number P1110, the Chamber however instructs the Registry to keep the document MFI'd pending a complete translation. With regard to the remaining 10 associated exhibits tendered by the Prosecution through the witness, the Chamber denies admission into evidence without prejudice. The Chamber will now turn to the second outstanding matter with regard to Witness Suljevic; namely, the admission of his comments chart, currently marked for identification as P890 and 39 related documents all tendered by the Prosecution from the bar table on the 11th of February, 2013. Following an order from the Chamber on the 11th of February, the Registry reserved 39 exhibit numbers for the documents related to the comments chart ranging from Exhibits P891 up to and including exhibit number P929. In court on the 11th of February, 2013, the Defence objected to the admission of the comments chart on the basis that it is of limited probative value and to the admission of the underlying documents on the basis that the witness does not have any personal knowledge of them. The objection relating to the underlying documents was repeated in the Defence's written submissions, dated the 28th of June, 2013. Therein, the Defence further added that the witness's lack of knowledge of the document means that he is unable to authentic them. The Chamber has analysed the comments chart in light of Rules 89(C) and (D) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence and notes at the outset that all documents referred to in it are alleged VRS military documents in relation to which the witness identified the type of ammunition discussed. In various instances, the witness also made reference to paragraphs of Exhibit P889, his consolidated statement of the 9th of February, 2010, in which he discussed his investigations into the types of projectiles and other ammunition. Moreover, during his testimony on the 11th of February, the witness affirmed the document's authenticity and his comments therein. Having analysed the documents, the Chamber considers that they meet the standard of reliability necessary for admission. Considering the above, the Chamber finds the comments chart and underlying documents to be relevant to and probative of the alleged use of weaponry by the VRS. The Chamber therefore admits Exhibit P890 and its underlying documents ranging from exhibit number P891 up to and including exhibit number 929 into evidence. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. We adjourn for the day and after we've heard from Mr. Lukic how much time he still would need tomorrow, we'll after that resume tomorrow morning, 24th of July, 2013, in this same courtroom III. Mr. Lukic, the last word is yours today.
